findings.description: Valid configured companion_chain lists are never accepted. The function pipes JSON arrays from yq into `jq -rn`, but `-R` makes `inputs` raw strings, so `.value[0]` inspects the first character of the JSON text rather than the parsed tag array. Every element is classified as non-hop and a valid operator chain falls back to defaults.
findings.failure_mode: A production config such as `companion_chain.openai: [codex-headless]` is ignored, causing the script to run the default companion chain instead of the operator-selected chain. That can dispatch the wrong provider/model and violate the documented configuration contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the yq JSON instead of reading raw strings, e.g. remove `-R` from jq and consume parsed inputs, or keep raw mode but call `fromjson` before indexing each element. Add a test that a valid list produces the configured hop names.

findings.description: process_findings creates a fresh mktemp file for _ADV_REPAIR_SKIP_FILE on every call and overwrites the global with the new path. No removal of the file (or of the previous call's file) appears in the diff. When _ADVERSARIAL_WORKDIR is unset (unit-test harness, or any call path before the run workdir exists) the file lands in $TMPDIR or /tmp, where no workdir sweep will ever remove it.
findings.failure_mode: Repeated runs or test invocations without a run workdir accumulate adv-repair-skipped.XXXXXX files in /tmp; within one run, a second process_findings call (companion walker, re-validation) orphans the first file's path so even a workdir-scoped cleanup cannot name it.
findings.suggested_fix: Create the skip file only under _ADVERSARIAL_WORKDIR (skip the feature with a log line when it is unset), or register the path in the EXIT cleanup and `rm -f` the previous value before reassigning the global.

findings.description: The _xid renumbering block runs for both branches ("whatever the branch"). On the schema-enforced path a whitespace-only or otherwise non-token `id` is therefore rewritten to a fresh DISS-NNN and tagged id_derived: true before validate_finding sees it. The new `(.id | test("\\S"))` gate added to validate_finding is thus unreachable for any string id, and the stated rule for the enforced path (no normalisation, so a wire-schema/prompt drift is surfaced as a rejection) is bypassed for the id field: a blank id from an enforced payload is accepted and logged only as "not a safe token", never as a drift rejection.
findings.failure_mode: A schema-enforced voice that starts emitting blank or malformed ids is silently repaired per finding instead of producing rejected_summary rows, so the drift the enforced path is meant to expose goes unnoticed; the log line also misdescribes a blank id as a non-token.
findings.suggested_fix: On the schema-enforced branch, skip the \u0001 (unsafe/blank) renumbering and let validate_finding reject the finding (keep the duplicate-id and DISS-C- renumbering, which are not schema concerns); or, if renumbering is intended there, state it in the branch comment and have validate_finding's id gate removed as dead code.

findings.description: `validated_findings=$(_adv_jq_pair "$validated_findings" "$validated" '$a + [$b]')` has no failure guard. If validate_anchor ever yields a non-JSON or multi-value output for one finding, _adv_jq_pair refuses ("two values expected" or a parse error) and the accumulator collapses to an empty string; every later iteration then fails the array-literal parse as well, so all remaining valid findings are lost and the final envelope assembly reads an empty accumulator. The pre-change --argjson form had the same collapse, but the new helper makes the loss deterministic and loud for every subsequent finding rather than only the one that misbehaved.
findings.failure_mode: One malformed validate_anchor result silently drops every validated finding after it (or aborts process_findings under errexit), producing an envelope with fewer findings than were accepted and no rejected_summary row for them.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture into a temporary and keep the previous accumulator on failure: `_nv=$(_adv_jq_pair ... ) && validated_findings="$_nv" || { log "WARN: finding $i could not be appended — kept out"; rejected_count=$((rejected_count+1)); }`, and write a sidecar/rejected_summary row for the finding so the loss is said.

findings.description: `repair_metadata_json` binds `rhs` with `--argjson`, but the value is a plain space-separated string from `sort | tr | sed`, or an empty string when no repair hops were skipped. `jq --argjson rhs ""` and `jq --argjson rhs "claude:over_budget"` are invalid JSON, so envelope construction fails even on normal runs with no skip file.
findings.failure_mode: A review can complete validation and then abort while building metadata, producing no adversarial envelope. With `set -e`, the failed command substitution can terminate the script before `write_output`; without it, later `--argjson repairmeta "$repair_metadata_json"` receives an empty/non-JSON value and fails as well.
findings.suggested_fix: Change `--argjson rhs ...` to `--arg rhs ...` and keep the existing jq expression treating `$rhs` as a string, or emit a real JSON array from the shell and adjust the jq expression accordingly.

findings.description: In the takeover section the verdict `stuck` is emitted whenever `mv -- "$dir" "$_stale"` fails, which conflates two different states: the dead lock directory could not be renamed (permissions), and the directory vanished between the `[[ -d "$dir" ]] || { echo released; }` check and the rename (the holder released unserialised after its own 5 s flock wait, or without flock installed). After the loop, `stuck` is mapped to `_adv_run_lock_unguarded` and the run proceeds. If a `stuck` verdict lands on round 3 and the round-4 `mkdir` then loses to a fresh run that took the freed key, the code reports a dead lock that could not be moved aside and runs unguarded beside a live holder, whereas the same round-4 loss after `takeover`/`released` is correctly refused.
findings.failure_mode: Two live runs for the same (sprint, gate) write the single-writer envelope and sidecars concurrently, in exactly the window the lock exists to close. Requires the vanish-during-section race to occur on round 3 specifically plus a lost round-4 mkdir, so the likelihood is low.
findings.suggested_fix: After the failed `mv`, distinguish the states: `if mv ...; then ...; echo takeover; elif [[ ! -d "$dir" ]]; then echo released; else echo stuck; fi`. `released` already routes a lost round-4 mkdir to a refusal rather than an unguarded run.

findings.description: The queue-phase budget is `_adv_cli_hop_bound(cur) + 30` for every hop in phase `queue`. `_walk_companion_chain` puts an HTTP hop whose catalog fallback_chain reaches a CLI binary into `queue` too, but `_adv_with_cli_lock` waits for that hop's lock only `${CONF_TIMEOUT:-60}` (the non-`*-headless` branch), not `_adv_cli_hop_bound`. For a listed HTTP hop with no headless_timeout_seconds the bound is max(connect,10)+max(read,600) = 610, so the queue budget is 640 s regardless of the configured call timeout. The wait-cap and post-budget rules in the same hunk charge that lock wait as `t` (the call timeout), so the three rules disagree for this hop class.
findings.failure_mode: With `timeout_seconds` configured above ~640 s (plausible on this host, where CLI hops run 910 s), a companion on e.g. `claude-bedrock` queued behind the primary's `claude -p` is reaped by main at 640 s with `phase 'queue' deadline` while `flock -w` would still legitimately wait up to CONF_TIMEOUT. The voice is dropped as lock_wait/timeout although its own budget allowed the wait.
findings.suggested_fix: In the `queue` branch, derive the budget from the same rule `_adv_with_cli_lock` uses: when `_adv_hop_canon "$cur"` is not `*-headless`, use `${CONF_TIMEOUT:-60} + 30` (or the walker's actual `$timeout`, published alongside `companion.current`); keep `_adv_cli_hop_bound ... strict` only for `*-headless` hops.

findings.description: `_adv_cli_hop_bound ... strict` is meant to return 1 on any failed catalog read so `_companion_deadline_why` never latches the 610 fallback over a yq hiccup (thirty-fourth run fix). But the first catalog read on that path is inside `_adv_hop_canon` → `_adv_alias_target`, where a yq failure is swallowed (`|| t=""`). For a hop spelled as a catalog alias, a transient yq failure leaves the hop un-canonicalised; the subsequent `has()` read legitimately answers `false` for the alias name, `from_catalog` stays false, and the function returns 0 with `_ADV_CLI_HOP_TIMEOUT` — which the caller then caches as the queue budget for the rest of that hop.
findings.failure_mode: An aliased `*-headless` companion hop with a 910 s catalog bound gets a cached 640 s queue budget after one failed alias read and is reaped inside its legitimate lock wait — the exact shape a3 DISS-C-002 was meant to close, reopened for aliased spellings only.
findings.suggested_fix: Give `_adv_alias_target`/`_adv_hop_canon` a strict mode (or return 1 when the yq alias read itself fails, distinguishing a failed read from `null`), and have `_adv_cli_hop_bound` propagate that as `return 1` when `strict` is set.

findings.description: The per-binary lock directory is `${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}}/loa-headless-locks-<uid>`, with `~/.cache/loa/headless-locks-<uid>` only as a fallback when that path is not ours. Two dissents run by the same user in different environments — one from a systemd session (XDG_RUNTIME_DIR set) and one from cron/CI/ssh-without-session (unset) — therefore lock in different directories (`/run/user/<uid>/...` vs `/tmp/...`, both legitimately ours) and never see each other's `claude.lock`.
findings.failure_mode: Two `claude -p` invocations overlap on the host (the KF-037 contention shape the lock exists to prevent) with no WARN, because each process believes it holds the only lock.
findings.suggested_fix: Use one environment-independent location as the primary (e.g. always the private `~/.cache/loa/headless-locks-<uid>` path, which is already created 0700 and ownership-checked), and treat `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` as an optimisation only when a stable per-user path cannot be made.

findings.description: comp_status is set to "succeeded" solely because companion.result.json exists and parses as a JSON object. Neither companion.status (read a few lines earlier and then used only for the failure class) nor the companion envelope's own metadata.status is consulted. Every other envelope this script writes carries metadata.status in {reviewed, api_failure, malformed_response, ...}; the same writer behind the companion's result path can therefore leave a well-formed object whose status is a failure (the CMP-168 shape, mirrored onto the companion side). The success branch then folds zero findings, sums its spend, and — when the primary also failed — promotes the whole envelope to status "reviewed" with the note "findings are the companion voice's alone".
findings.failure_mode: A run in which both voices failed can be published as a clean, reviewed envelope with no findings, so the gate passes vacuously and the companion is recorded as counted_as sole_voice / independent_voice with a FAILED envelope feeding verdict quality.
findings.suggested_fix: Gate comp_status="succeeded" on all three signals: the result object exists, companion.status is "succeeded" (or absent), and $cres.metadata.status is not in ("api_failure","malformed_response"). Otherwise fall through to the failed branch and let _companion_failure_class name it (the status/rc files are already in hand).

findings.description: The MODELINV window bounds are read as `cat hop_started_iso || cat started_iso || echo epoch` and `cat hop_ended_iso || cat ended_iso || echo far-future`. `cat` on a present-but-empty file exits 0 with empty output, so the fallbacks never fire for an empty state file; only the third line patches one shape (hop_started non-empty, hop_ended empty). CMP-134 gave companion.current the missing-file fallback for exactly this class, but the four ISO files here still treat empty as a value. An empty _since opens the window at the start of the ledger, so _companion_ledger_message can return another voice's or an earlier run's row for the same model — the misattribution rounds 37/38 closed for the lock_wait case.
findings.failure_mode: With hop_started_iso cleared or truncated (reaped at the moment the walker rotates its per-hop state), the companion's last_error and failure_class are derived from a row that belongs to the primary's shared hop or a previous run, and that text is logged and summarised as this voice's diagnostic.
findings.suggested_fix: Read each bound through a small helper that returns the first file with -s content (e.g. `_first_nonempty_file a b` then the literal default), and drop the special-case third line. Add a companion case with an empty hop_started_iso beside a non-empty started_iso asserting the window opens at started_iso.

findings.description: `_adv_range_diff` passes the user-controlled diff range as a positional argument before `--`. If `--diff-range` begins with `-`, Git parses it as another `git diff` option rather than a revision range. That can redirect output, alter diff semantics, or trigger unexpected modes before the script parses the review content.
findings.failure_mode: A crafted or accidental range such as `--output=/path/file` or another git-diff option can change where the diff is written or make the reviewer consume an empty/misleading diff, violating the review scope contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate `diff_range` before calling `_adv_range_diff` so only the intended revision grammar is accepted, then pass it in a way Git treats as a revision, for example after strict allowlisting of `rev...rev` / `rev..rev` forms. Reject any range beginning with `-` before invoking `git diff`.

findings.description: _adv_kill_tree cancels the CONT watchdog with `kill -TERM -- -$pgid`, but on every signal/exit path the reapers run after `trap '' INT TERM` (_adv_cleanup_on_exit sets it as its first statement, and the report states both INT/TERM trap bodies begin the same way). A process forked while SIGTERM is ignored inherits SIG_IGN, and POSIX forbids a non-interactive sh from trapping or resetting a signal ignored on entry; `sleep` inherits SIG_IGN across exec as well. So the `setsid sh -c '...; sleep; kill -CONT ...'` watchdog (and the no-setsid subshell fallback) cannot be cancelled: the TERM is silently dropped and the watchdog always fires after ${_ADV_CONT_WATCHDOG_SECONDS:-10} s. This defeats the thirty-third-run fix whose whole point was that a pid resumed by our own CONT pass, then stopped by its owner or recycled, is never resumed later. The watchdog is also spawned via `$(...)` from the reaper, so it outlives the script as a detached orphan for the full delay.
findings.failure_mode: Every INT/TERM/EXIT reap leaves one or two uncancellable `sh`+`sleep` pairs that, 10 s after the run has exited, send SIGCONT to every pid of the former companion/primary tree. A pid recycled in that window to a process its owner deliberately stopped (job-control Ctrl-Z, a debugger, another reaper's freeze) is resumed by us. Test sweeps and pid-scoped assertions also see stray processes for 10 s after each signalled run.
findings.suggested_fix: Cancel with a signal that cannot be ignored: `kill -KILL -- "$x"` for the setsid group (both `sh` and `sleep` die) and `kill -KILL "$!"` in the fallback (the CONT loop lives in the subshell, so killing it is a complete cancel). Alternatively, have the watchdog poll a cancel file in the workdir before each CONT. Do not try `trap - TERM` inside the child: a signal ignored at entry cannot be reset there, and restoring default TERM in the parent would reopen the second-signal window the `trap ''` closes. Add a bats case that runs the reaper from inside a `trap '' INT TERM` context and asserts no watchdog survives the kill_tree return.

findings.description: `_ADV_CONT_WATCHDOG_SECONDS` is read raw into `sleep "$0"`, unlike every sibling knob (grace, wait caps, budgets) which goes through `_conf_uint`. An empty, non-numeric or negative value makes `sleep` fail immediately, so the watchdog runs its CONT loop at once, while _adv_kill_tree still has the tree frozen and before the token read and the TERM pass. The freeze that the token-while-frozen rule (a4 DISS-C-002) depends on is then silently absent.
findings.failure_mode: With a malformed knob, descendants are resumed between the STOP and TERM passes; a pid can exit and be freed before its token is taken, so the KILL identity check is computed against the wrong process, which is the race the freeze was introduced to close.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve the delay once via `_conf_uint "LOA_ADVERSARIAL_CONT_WATCHDOG_SECONDS" ... <default 10> <floor 1>` (or the existing `_ADV_CONT_WATCHDOG_SECONDS` name) and pass the validated integer; refuse or clamp values below the longest expected freeze pass.

findings.description: The subshell unsets GIT_DIFF_OPTS and GIT_ATTR_SOURCE but leaves git's repository-discovery environment in place (GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_COMMON_DIR, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY, GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES, GIT_NAMESPACE). verdict-derive's `_vd_committed` already clears this set for the same reason. When the script is launched from a git hook or by a wrapper that exports an absolute GIT_DIR (git sets GIT_DIR/GIT_INDEX_FILE for hooks), `git -C "$1" diff` and `hash-object` operate on that repository, not on the tree at `$1`; GIT_NAMESPACE silently changes which commits the range's ref names resolve to.
findings.failure_mode: The reviewed diff and the empty-tree attribute source are taken from a different repository or ref namespace than PROJECT_ROOT, so both voices review the wrong change while `metadata.scope.diff_oids` records oids consistent with that wrong repository.
findings.suggested_fix: In the same `( unset ... )` subshell, also unset GIT_DIR GIT_WORK_TREE GIT_COMMON_DIR GIT_INDEX_FILE GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES GIT_NAMESPACE GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES (mirroring `_vd_committed`), and apply the same set wherever `_ADV_RANGE_OIDS` is resolved so the oids and the diff come from one discovery.

findings.description: The new flag-presence rule (comment: 'a flag's presence, never its value, decides') is enforced for --record-fallback (empty value is a usage error) and for --reason without --record-fallback, but not for --since. `--since) fallback_since="${2:-}"; _since_given=1; ...` followed by `_adv_record_fallback ... "$fallback_since"` means `--record-fallback failed --since ""` (or `--since` as the last argument) is accepted and passed through as 'no --since'. The --since guard is what refuses to displace an envelope newer than the aborted run's start (CMP-146); a skill that composes the command from a captured start timestamp that came back empty loses that guard silently and the failed record displaces whatever envelope stands, including a later retry's completed one.
findings.failure_mode: An automated caller passes an empty --since value; the fallback record is written without the newer-envelope refusal and overwrites a completed envelope with a failed record (moved to .prev, not restored).
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the --record-fallback check: `if [[ -n "$_since_given" && -z "$fallback_since" ]]; then error "--since needs a timestamp"; exit 2; fi` before the `_adv_record_fallback` call, so an empty value is a usage error rather than a dropped guard.

findings.description: In the --diff-range block main registers `trap 'command rm -f -- "$_ADV_RANGE_DIFF"' EXIT`. A few lines later, after the workdir is created, main registers `trap '_adv_cleanup_on_exit' EXIT`, which replaces (not chains) the earlier EXIT trap. From that point the range-diff temp file under TMPDIR is removed only if `_adv_cleanup_on_exit` (outside this diff) knows about `_ADV_RANGE_DIFF`. The diff itself gives no evidence that it does; if it does not, every --diff-range run leaves a copy of the reviewed diff in TMPDIR.
findings.failure_mode: Each --diff-range run (the skills' default path since the audit's git-diff grant was replaced) leaks a `adversarial-range-XXXXXX` file containing the full reviewed diff in a shared TMPDIR.
findings.suggested_fix: Either have `_adv_cleanup_on_exit` remove `${_ADV_RANGE_DIFF:-}` (guarded with `|| true`), or move the range file into the run workdir once it exists, so the single cleanup trap covers it. Add a test asserting no `adversarial-range-*` file survives a --diff-range run.

findings.description: The synthetic 'every hop of the primary chain was ceded to the companion' envelope hardcodes `status: "api_failure", degraded: false` for both gates. process_findings sets `degraded: true` for an audit API failure (the nineteenth-run refutation of a3 C-003 states this rule). When the subsequent fold fails (`companion_voice.status: fold_failed`), the audit envelope written to disk says `api_failure` with `degraded: false`, which the audit gate's DEGRADED_SECURITY_REVIEW rule and verdict-derive read differently from a process_findings-produced api_failure envelope.
findings.failure_mode: An audit run whose primary chain was entirely ceded and whose fold then failed writes an api_failure envelope with degraded:false, inconsistent with every other audit api_failure envelope and with the audit resource's degraded rule.
findings.suggested_fix: Set `degraded` from the gate in the synthetic: `--argjson degraded "$([[ "$type" == audit ]] && echo true || echo false)"`, matching process_findings' api_failure shape; or route the synthetic through the same helper process_findings uses to build its failure envelope.

findings.description: _vd_committed decides that a sidecar newer than a pre-FR-2 envelope is history when `git ls-files --error-unmatch` and `git diff --quiet HEAD -- <name>` both pass. The subshell unsets git's repository/discovery environment but leaves the user's diff configuration in force: `diff.external` / `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` and attribute-driven `diff=<driver>` with a `command`, plus pathspec globbing. With an external diff configured (difftastic, delta and similar are common in global config) and a stat-dirty index entry for the sidecar (a `touch`, a checkout on a different filesystem, a changed mtime after the thirty-fifth run's own scenario), recent git versions run the external program under `--exit-code`/`--quiet` and, without `diff.trustExitCode`, report a change. The committed sidecar is then classed as a later run's rows and counted, which is exactly the false INCONSISTENT on historical audit sprints that `_vd_committed` was added to remove. A sidecar name holding `[`, `*` or `?` would also be matched as a glob by both git commands.
findings.failure_mode: On a host with a user-level external diff driver, a committed, byte-identical rejected sidecar beside a legacy envelope is reported as 'newer than it … those rows are counted', the feedback file that never triaged those rows reads INCONSISTENT (exit 1), and historical sprints lose their verdicts again. Low likelihood: it needs both the external-diff config and a stat-dirty index entry; the failure direction is fail-closed.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the history check independent of the user's diff configuration: `git -C … --literal-pathspecs -c diff.external= diff --no-ext-diff --no-textconv --quiet HEAD -- "${1##*/}"` (and `--literal-pathspecs` on the `ls-files` call). Optionally export `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` inside the subshell so a read-only verdict script never writes the caller's index.

findings.description: The security_audit budget_cents comment restates the repair wall-budget floor as "two of the heaviest hop's charges at least", while the code_review block it points to says "never under two of the heaviest hop's charges plus a timeout" (the implementation report, round 1t, matches the code_review wording). The code_review block also says a pin "below a hop's charge is warned", whereas the report (round 1v, CMP-235) records "a pinned repair budget below every CLI charge warns at load" — below the lightest CLI charge is a different condition from below any hop's charge. Finally both blocks derive the default from "THIS block's timeout_seconds" but LOA_ADVERSARIAL_REPAIR_BUDGET_SECONDS is a single env knob; neither comment says one pin governs both gates.
findings.failure_mode: An operator who sizes the env pin from the audit block's text under-budgets by one timeout; one who relies on the documented load-time warning to catch a too-small pin may get none when the pin sits between the lightest and heaviest CLI charge; a pin tuned for code_review's timeout silently governs security_audit too. Repairs are then pre-empted, payloads land in rejected_summary and the sidecar, and verdict-derive demands triage bullets — degraded dissent rather than a crash.
findings.suggested_fix: In security_audit replace the paraphrase with "repair wall budget: code_review's rule applied to this block's timeout_seconds" and nothing more; state the warn condition exactly as _adv_repair_wall_for implements it (pick one phrasing and use it in both blocks); add to both blocks that the env pin applies to both gates at once.

findings.description: The companion_chain override block (and its 'used as given — no PATH filter' semantics) is documented only under code_review. The security_audit block's new companion_voice comment says 'see code_review' for the voice rule but never mentions that companion_chain is read per block (implementation report: 'operator companion_chain per block (CMP-13)').
findings.failure_mode: An operator places companion_chain once under code_review (for example to route the companion onto claude-bedrock around KF-037) and expects it to apply to audits; audits keep the default chain. On a host where the default chain has no route, every audit records companion_voice {planned: false, reason: no_route} and is DEGRADED_SECURITY_REVIEW while the operator believes the override is in effect.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a one-line pointer under security_audit, e.g. '# companion_chain: per block — same shape as code_review's; a code_review override does not reach audits'.

findings.description: Both budget_cents comments say '(a malformed value fails closed as 0)'. The implementation report (sixteenth run) records the behaviour as refusing the run with exit 4 and a JSON status. 'as 0' reads either as 'treated as a 0-cent budget' or as 'exits 0'; in a file read by shell-tooling operators the second reading is natural and inverts the meaning. The comment also never states that an explicit budget_cents: 0 refuses every dispatch, though 0 conventionally means 'no cap'.
findings.failure_mode: An operator reads the malformed-value path as a silent exit-0 and does not check the run's status; or sets budget_cents: 0 intending no cap and every dissent is refused before dispatch, so with the gate enforced no review or audit can write its COMPLETED marker until the value is changed.
findings.suggested_fix: Reword to '(a malformed or zero value refuses the run before any dispatch — exit 4, status in the JSON; there is no unlimited setting)'.

findings.description: The stale sweep decides an owner is dead once at the top of its per-marker loop (`_sweep_alive "$p" && continue`) and removes the marker only at the bottom (`(( left )) || rm -f -- "$m"`). Between those two points a sibling test's setup can start with that very pid (pid reuse after a crashed run), find its OUT_DIR already renamed away by the sweep, and in `_place_marker` take the EEXIST branch: the stale marker is not foreign, so `mv -f` replaces it with the live run's marker. The sweep then finishes emptying the renamed directory, sees `left == 0`, and `rm -f`s the marker it originally judged stale, which is now the live test's marker. The liveness verdict is never re-checked against the file that is actually deleted.
findings.failure_mode: Under `bats --jobs` (or any concurrent run of this suite over one checkout) with a prior crashed run and a reused pid, the live test's a2a directory runs unmarked. No data is wrongly deleted and the test's own teardown still removes its directory, but if that test is killed mid-run the leftover `sprint-comp-<pid>` is permanent: no sweep will ever claim it (no marker) and the next run that lands on that pid fails setup with `stands and is not this suite's` until an operator removes it by hand.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-check liveness immediately before removing the marker, and only remove the marker you read: e.g. capture the marker's inode (`stat -c %i` / `ls -i`) or its full content when first judged stale, then at the bottom do `if ! _sweep_alive "$p" && [[ "$(stat …)" == "$saved" ]]; then rm -f -- "$m"; fi`. Alternatively have `_place_marker` write a fresh content token (e.g. append the start token from `_sweep_start "$$"`) and have the sweep `rm` only when the marker still carries the token it read at the top.

findings.description: The second leg stubs `_adv_kill_tree` to hand the inner reaper a hard-coded pid `999999` with token `tFROZEN` as a member of the companion's tree. On 64-bit Linux `kernel.pid_max` defaults to 4194304, so 999999 can be a live process owned by the same user (another CI job, the operator's own shell). After the grace the reaper walks `_ADV_REAP_TREE_PIDS` and KILLs every pid whose token still matches; the only thing between this fixture and `kill -KILL 999999` is the same-process token check that CMP-62, CMP-82 and CMP-100 exist to guard against regressions in. The test asserts the token bookkeeping (`_ADV_REAP_TREE_TOKENS`, `_ADV_REAP_TREE_PIDS`) but never asserts 999999 was left alone, so a regression in that check would kill an unrelated host process while the test stays green.
findings.failure_mode: A regression in `_adv_kill_same` or the post-grace re-collection, plus a live same-user process at pid 999999, makes a run of the suite SIGKILL that process. Nothing in the test turns red.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a pid that cannot exist (`$(( $(cat /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max 2>/dev/null || echo 4194304) + 1 ))`), or better an owned `sleep 30` carrying a deliberately wrong token, as CMP-62's last leg does, and assert it survives the reap.

findings.description: The run-lock half of the title is checked with `[ ! -d "$(cat "$T/lockdir")" ]`, where `lockdir` is filled from `$_ADV_RUN_LOCK_DIR` inside the subshell. When `_adv_take_run_lock` fails open (no sha256sum/shasum, lock directory not ours, the paths CMP-93 pins) that variable is empty, the file is empty, and `[ ! -d "" ]` is true. The leg then passes without any lock having been taken or released. The workdir leg is sound; the lock leg can pass vacuously on exactly the hosts where the fail-open path is live.
findings.failure_mode: On a host where the run lock fails open, a cleanup that skips `_adv_release_run_lock` after a masked second INT/TERM is not detected by this test.
findings.suggested_fix: Assert `[ -s "$T/lockdir" ]` after the subshell (or `[ -d "$_ADV_RUN_LOCK_DIR" ]` inside it before the traps are set), mirroring CMP-93's owned-directory leg which asserts `[ -n "$_ADV_RUN_LOCK_DIR" ]` and `[ -d ... ]` as two statements.

findings.description: CMP-97 redefines `_adv_proc_start` to return a constant and CMP-82 to a t1/t2 toggle keyed on `$T/reused`; neither restores the original. CMP-62 and CMP-71 do restore via `eval "$_orig_proc_start"`, but only on the success path: the restore line is skipped whenever an earlier assertion trips errexit. bats runs `teardown` in the same process as the test body, so teardown's sweeps run against the stub. The implementation report says those sweeps use start tokens ('sweeps name their renames with a start token', 'stale sweeps that respect hidepid'), and CMP-90's comment shows the authors already hit this class of leak for `cat` and routed it through `command cat`. The same seam is open for `_adv_proc_start` and `_adv_kill_tree` (CMP-82, CMP-109). Teardown itself is not in this chunk, so the exact consequence could not be confirmed.
findings.failure_mode: Under `bats -j` or beside a live dissent, a teardown that compares recorded tokens against the stubbed `_adv_proc_start` judges every live holder recycled (constant token) or never dead (t2 forever), so the sweep removes a sibling's live a2a or lock directory or leaves stale ones behind, while the test that caused it reports green.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture `declare -f _adv_proc_start` and `declare -f _adv_kill_tree` in `setup` and `eval` them back as the first statements of `teardown`, so every test's overrides are undone regardless of where the test stopped; the per-test `eval "$_orig_proc_start"` lines then become redundant.

findings.description: The third leg forks a TERM-ignoring `sleep 300` named `loa-cmp30-stubborn-$$`, SIGSTOPs it, and relies on the single `_adv_reap_companion` statement to KILL it. The test's own `kill -CONT; kill -KILL` fallback runs only if the process is still alive at the probe after that statement. If `_adv_reap_companion` itself returns non-zero (the failure the second leg of this very test guards against), bats errexit aborts the test before the probe. The in-line comment states teardown ends holders with TERM, which this process ignores and, being stopped, does not even receive until a CONT; a stopped `sleep` never runs its timer, so it does not expire after 300 s either.
findings.failure_mode: A regression that makes the re-entered reaper return non-zero leaves a permanently stopped `loa-cmp30-stubborn-<pid>` process on the CI or dev host after every run of the suite, invisible to the TERM teardown and to `pkill` with the default signal.
findings.suggested_fix: Have teardown resume and KILL HOLDER_PIDS (`kill -CONT` then `kill -KILL`) instead of TERM, or make the leg's cleanup unconditional: `rc=0; _adv_reap_companion || rc=$?; kill -CONT "$q" 2>/dev/null || true; kill -KILL "$q" 2>/dev/null || true; [ "$rc" = 0 ]`.

findings.description: The 'publishes its hop and phase whole' half of the title is proven by a source-text grep over `declare -f _walk_companion_chain` for the literal `> "$workdir/companion.(current|phase)"` and over `_adv_invoke_hop` for `> "$_ADV_PHASE_FILE"`. `declare -f` prints variable references as written, so a truncating write spelled `"${workdir}/companion.phase"`, through any other local, or to an unquoted path passes the lint. The `_adv_put_state` leg that follows exercises the helper in isolation and says nothing about whether the walker calls it. The behavioural half (the verdict waits on an empty `current`) is sound; the atomicity half rests on a brittle lint.
findings.failure_mode: A later edit that writes `companion.phase` or `companion.current` with a plain redirection under a different spelling is not caught; the primary's shared-hop wait can again read a torn hop name and run the hop the companion is moving onto.
findings.suggested_fix: Either widen the lint to any redirection whose target names the file regardless of variable spelling (e.g. `grep -E '>+ *"?[^ ]*companion\.(current|phase)'`), or assert behaviourally: wrap `_adv_put_state` in a counting stub, run a two-hop walk, and expect one call per hop/phase transition with no `*.tmp*` left behind.

findings.description: The setsid leg of CMP-204 never asserts that the victim was actually frozen. It polls up to 3 s for a `T*` state, then polls up to 4 s for it to clear, then asserts `!= T*`. If `_adv_kill_tree` fails at once inside the `setsid bash -c` body (the body carries only four functions via `declare -f`; any other helper `_adv_kill_tree` or `_adv_tree_pids` calls, such as a logger or a pid-liveness check, is `command not found` there), the victim is never stopped, both loops fall through immediately and the final check passes. CMP-193 guards the same scenario with an explicit "the stub never ran inside the freeze" assertion; this leg has no equivalent, so the property it claims to pin (the CONT watchdog survives a process-group KILL of the reviewer) is not actually exercised on a host where the inlined body cannot run.
findings.failure_mode: A regression that drops the watchdog's own-session detachment, or a refactor that adds a helper to the kill-tree path, leaves this leg green while the guarantee it names is gone; a frozen `claude -p` can then hold the per-binary lock indefinitely after a group kill, exactly the failure the test exists to catch.
findings.suggested_fix: Record whether `T*` was observed (set a flag in the first loop) and fail with a message when it was not, mirroring CMP-193; or run the body through `bash -c "$(declare -f $(compgen -A function _adv_))..."` so every script helper is present, and additionally assert the watchdog pid appeared (e.g. via the `wd-calls`-style seam used in CMP-209).

findings.description: CMP-210 ages the `companion.phase` file with `touch -d "@$(( now - 700 ))"` (three times). `-d @<epoch>` is GNU coreutils syntax; BSD/macOS `touch -d` takes an ISO-8601 string and rejects `@…`. The implementation report records that the tenth run removed every GNU-only primitive (`date +%s%N`, `touch -d`, unguarded `flock`) from this suite as a standing rule, and CMP-183 in this same slice is titled as pinning the suite's own portability floor. This test reintroduces the retired primitive with no `skip` guard.
findings.failure_mode: On a non-GNU host the three `touch` calls exit non-zero under bats errexit and CMP-210 reports red for a reason unrelated to the queue-phase bound it tests, breaking the suite's documented contract that GNU-only tooling is either avoided or skipped.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the python3 the suite already requires (`python3 -c 'import os,sys; t=int(sys.argv[2]); os.utime(sys.argv[1],(t,t))' "$T/dq210/companion.phase" $((now-700))`), or drive `_companion_deadline_why` through its fake-clock seam the repair-loop tests use, so no mtime manipulation is needed.

findings.description: `_claim_sprint_dir` runs `chmod u+w -- "$d"` before `find -mindepth 1 -delete` and its comment says this is "the sweep's rule" (CMP-187's `chmod a-w` on a killed run). The sweep in this same file does not implement that rule: `_sweep_stale_suite_dirs` renames the dead owner's directory to `.reap-<pid>-<tok>` and then runs `find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete 2>/dev/null || true; rmdir "$d" 2>/dev/null || left=1` with no permission repair, and teardown's own-dir path (`find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete; rmdir "$d"`) likewise does not restore write permission. A killed run whose sprint-norm directory holds a non-writable subtree therefore fails `find -delete`, sets `left=1`, keeps the marker, and on every later teardown the `.reap-*` entry is re-examined (the dead reaper pid lets it through) and fails again — the leftover and its marker persist indefinitely, which is the accumulation the header comment says the sweep prevents.
findings.failure_mode: A read-only subtree under `grimoires/loa/a2a/sprint-norm-<pid>` left by a killed test is never cleared: every subsequent run's teardown re-attempts the delete, fails silently (`2>/dev/null || true`), and the `.reap-<pid>-<tok>` directory plus `.sprint-norm-<pid>.owner` marker accumulate in the checkout's a2a directory. In teardown's own-dir path the unguarded `find -delete` fails the test instead.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply the same rule the claim path uses: before `find "$d" -mindepth 1 -delete` in `_sweep_stale_suite_dirs` (after the `mv` to `.reap-*`) and in teardown's own-dir branch, run `chmod -R u+w -- "$d" 2>/dev/null || true` (or `find "$d" -type d ! -perm -u+w -exec chmod u+w {} +`). Alternatively drop the "the sweep's rule" wording from `_claim_sprint_dir` so the file does not claim a guarantee the sweep lacks.

findings.description: NRM-49 asserts `[ "$took" -lt 15 ]` on the real wall clock (`$SECONDS`) around a process_findings call that runs four ~120 KB payloads, two of which are rejected and go through the repair chain (lock acquisition, status files, sidecar writes). The suite's own rule, stated in NRM-26 and NRM-27 ("the test's own clock — no wall-clock margin to flake under load", run 23 c2b DISS-C-001), moved every timing expectation onto `_fake_repair_clock`; this test re-introduces a wall-clock bound. The round-20 dry run already saw NRM-22/NRM-26 race a whole-second budget guard under load, which is the same failure shape.
findings.failure_mode: On a loaded CI runner (parallel bats files, the dissent driver's other suites, a slow jq build) the four-payload run crosses 15 s and the test fails with no defect in the code under test; conversely the bound is loose enough that a quadratic regression on a single 120 KB payload (the 54 s case was 300 KB) can still pass well under 15 s, so the guard is both flaky and weak.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the wall-clock assertion with a structural one: pin that the rewritten predicates are linear by running the same payload at two sizes (e.g. 40k and 80k runs) under `_fake_repair_clock`-independent measurement of jq work, or assert the absence of the whole-string `gsub` directly in the extracted jq programs (grep the derive/clean filters for `gsub(` over the full string). If a timing bound is kept, use a per-size ratio (time(2n)/time(n) < 3) rather than an absolute 15 s, and document the slack rule the other tests follow.

findings.description: The operand lint in NRM-46 is an allowlist that must fail on every unreviewed way a payload-sized value reaches jq. Its environment rule is `(?:^|[\s;&|(])[A-Za-z_]\w*=\S*\s+(?:command\s+)?jq\b`. The `\S*` for the assigned value cannot span whitespace, so an env prefix whose quoted value contains a space — `P="x $finding_json" jq '$ENV.P'`, `P="${a} ${payload}" jq …`, or `P="$(printf '%s %s' …)" jq …` — never matches, and the `$ENV`/`env.` branch only fires when the jq program is on the same line (a program held in a variable, `jq -n "$prog"`, hides `$ENV.P`). The fixture set exercises only the single-token `P="$finding_json" jq` shape, so the gap is not covered by the lint's own positive/negative controls.
findings.failure_mode: A future edit that passes a payload through jq's environment with any whitespace in the value (or with the program in a variable) passes the lint silently; at runtime the envp string exceeds MAX_ARG_STRLEN and jq fails with E2BIG exactly like the argv case the lint exists to prevent (the exit-126 envelope loss from run 29).
findings.suggested_fix: In the environment rule, match the value as a shell word rather than `\S*`: allow quoted spans, e.g. `[A-Za-z_]\w*=(?:"(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*"|'[^']*'|\S)*\s+(?:command\s+)?jq\b`, and flag any such prefix whose value interpolates a name outside SMALL (reuse the existing `re.findall(r'\$\{?([A-Za-z_0-9]+)', …)` check). Add two fixtures to the NRM-46 control set: `P="x $finding_json" jq -n '$ENV.P'` must be caught, and `P="$model $i" jq -n '$ENV.P'` must pass.

findings.anchor: tests/unit/verdict-derive.bats:@test "verdict-derive: the section must carry one triage line per rejected payload — an empty or short section is INCONSISTENT (sprint-248 review, chunk b BLOCKING)"
findings.description: The third leg of this test (bullets before the section and in the next one) is the only review fixture in the file whose body omits the prose verdict marker 'Sprint 9 has been reviewed and approved.' that every sibling leg carries (s4 legs 1/2/4, s7, s11, s12, s16, _vd_approved_review). Without it the review gate's prose/trailer comparison can produce its own violation against the APPROVED trailer, so the guard `[ "$status" -eq 1 ] || { echo "bullets outside the section were counted: $output"; return 1; }` is satisfied whether or not the counter stopped at the next heading. The following substring assertion (`holds 1 top-level triage line(s)`…`2 rejected payload(s)`) still discriminates a counter that reads past the section, so the leg is not vacuous — but its diagnostic names the wrong cause on failure and the leg cannot show that the section-scoped count is the sole violation, which is exactly the class the s12 leg was corrected for ('the siblings' prose verdict marker too — the leg exercises the same prose/trailer path').
findings.failure_mode: A regression in the heading-scoped counter would be reported by this leg as the substring mismatch only; a reader following the custom message would be told bullets outside the section were counted when the exit-1 could equally come from the missing prose marker. A future edit that relaxes the substring assertion (e.g. to `[ "$status" -eq 1 ]` alone) would leave the leg green for the wrong reason.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `echo "Sprint 9 has been reviewed and approved. All acceptance criteria met."` to the third leg's body as the other legs do, and pin the claim under --json: `run _vd_quiet "$SCRIPT" --file "$d/engineer-feedback.md" --gate review --json; echo "$output" | jq -e '(.violations | length) == 1 and (.violations[0] | test("holds 1 top-level triage line.*2 rejected payload"))'` so the triage count is shown to be the only violation.

findings.anchor: tests/unit/verdict-derive.bats:verdict-derive: the suite never re-parses a path as shell source
findings.description: The negative fixture meant to prove detection of a `bash -c` program on the continuation line is missing any variable interpolation: `$'bash -c \\\n  "x"'`. `_vd_shsrc` only flags shell programs that interpolate variables, so this fixture is a constant program and should produce no hit.
findings.failure_mode: The test asserts `[ -n "$(_vd_shsrc "$f")" ]` for this fixture and will fail even when the lint is behaving as specified, breaking the verdict-derive unit suite.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the fixture to include an expansion on the continuation line, for example `$'bash -c \\\n  "x $d"'`, or remove it from the must-refuse list if constant continuation programs are intended to be allowed.

findings.description: In the s35 test ("an envelope as the writer before cycle-126 shaped it ... a sidecar git tracks"), the fixture helper g() resets only git's config environment (HOME, GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM) before running `git -C "$r" init -q`, `add -A`, `commit -q -m history`, `rm -q --cached`, and `add`. It leaves GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY, GIT_COMMON_DIR and GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES in place, which is exactly the set this same test proves the script under test unsets because hooks and dotfiles setups export them. Git exports GIT_DIR to hook processes (absolute for linked worktrees), pre-commit exports GIT_INDEX_FILE, and `GIT_DIR=~/.dotfiles GIT_WORK_TREE=~` is a common shell export. In any of those environments `git -C "$r" init` reinitialises the caller's repository instead of creating $r/.git, and `add -A` (whole work tree regardless of cwd) plus `commit` stage and commit into it: with GIT_WORK_TREE set that is the whole home directory; with GIT_DIR alone, $r becomes the work tree so every tracked path is staged as deleted and a2a/* added, then committed on the current branch; with only GIT_INDEX_FILE set, the pending commit's index is rewritten.
findings.failure_mode: Running the verdict-derive suite under an exported git repository environment (a hook, a linked-worktree hook, a dotfiles export) commits fixture files, mass deletions, or home-directory contents into an unrelated repository, or clobbers an in-progress commit's index; the test then fails with a misleading message or passes by accident.
findings.suggested_fix: Make g() hermetic the way the script is: run git in a subshell that unsets the discovery set, e.g. `g() { ( unset GIT_DIR GIT_WORK_TREE GIT_INDEX_FILE GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY GIT_COMMON_DIR GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES GIT_NAMESPACE GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES; HOME=/nonexistent GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/nonexistent command git -C "$r" -c user.email=t@t -c user.name=t "$@" ); }`, or pin GIT_DIR="$r/.git" GIT_WORK_TREE="$r" GIT_INDEX_FILE="$r/.git/index" explicitly; and assert `[[ -d "$r/.git" ]]` after init before any add.

findings.description: In the s27 FIFO leg ("a default sibling envelope that is not a regular file"), the watchdog subshell runs under bats' inherited errexit (its own comment says so) and guards its kill calls with `|| :`, but `wait "$s"` is unguarded and `sleep "${VD_FIFO_DEADLINE:-60}"` is unvalidated. Any nonzero return from wait other than the TERM-trap path (a non-numeric VD_FIFO_DEADLINE making sleep fail at once, or the sleep killed by a process sweep) exits the subshell before it writes fifo-expired, TERMs the reader's tree, or opens the FIFO's write end. A TERM delivered between `sleep ... &` and `s=$!` also runs the trap with $s empty and orphans the sleep. In the normal (fast-exit) path none of this is observable, so a dead watchdog is never noticed.
findings.failure_mode: If verdict-derive regresses to opening the FIFO sibling envelope, the test hangs indefinitely with no 'blocked on the FIFO' diagnostic because the deadline that was supposed to bound it exited silently; a misconfigured knob disables the deadline without any message.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate the knob before forking: `[[ ${VD_FIFO_DEADLINE:-60} =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || VD_FIFO_DEADLINE=60`; write `wait "$s" || :`; and begin the watchdog body with `set +e` (or assign `s` before installing the trap) so the body is fail-soft by construction instead of per-command guards.

findings.description: The embedded Python awk lint ("no awk program uses a POSIX character class") matches `(?<![\w.-])(?:[gmn]?awk\b|...)` anywhere in a non-comment line, not only in command position, and refuses every match whose next non-blank character is neither `-` nor `'` as 'an awk program not in single quotes'. Prose in a --help heredoc, an echo/printf diagnostic, a case label, or a string literal in verdict-derive.sh that mentions awk would therefore fail the suite, and the refusal text points at a quoting problem that does not exist. The lint runs against $SCRIPT unconditionally, so it is a trip wire for any future usage-text edit, and the skip-lookup regex covers only command -v/type/hash/which.
findings.failure_mode: A documentation-only change to the script's usage or warning text that names awk turns the verdict-derive suite red with a misleading 'not in single quotes' diagnostic; the real class check (the reason the lint exists) is unaffected.
findings.suggested_fix: Accept a match only in command position (line start or after `|`, `;`, `&&`, `||`, `$(`, `(`, `{`, `then`, `do`, or `name=$(`), skip heredoc bodies by tracking `<<[-]?['"]?WORD` to its terminator, and downgrade non-command mentions to a note rather than a refusal.

findings.description: The s33b2 test ("an empty rejected_sidecars entry, or one holding a newline ... never dropped silently or split into two names") pins exactly two 'malformed entry' violations and zero 'lists engineer-feedback.md' violations, but not the total violation count. If the script split the entry "adversarial-rejected-review-x.jsonl\nengineer-feedback.md" on the newline, the first half is a well-formed sidecar name that is listed but absent and would surface as a different violation (a missing listed sidecar) that nothing here asserts against. Sibling cases s22 and s28 pin `(.violations | length)` exactly; this one does not, so the 'never split' half of its title is only half-proved.
findings.failure_mode: A regression that splits a control-character entry and reports its first half as a listed-but-missing sidecar passes this test as long as the malformed count stays at two.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `(.violations | length) == 2` to the jq assertion, and optionally `(.violations | map(select(test("review-x.jsonl") and (test("malformed") | not))) | length) == 0` so any non-malformed mention of the split name fails the case.

findings.description: The new `--json` leg runs `bash -c "\"$SCRIPT\" --file \"$T/r.md\" --gate review --review-file \"$T/r.md\" --json 2>/dev/null"`, interpolating two filesystem paths into a shell command string. The reviewer context records that the sibling verdict-derive suite was deliberately moved off this exact pattern ("82 verdict-derive cases off `bash -c`", the `bash -c` lint) because a path containing `"`, `$`, a backtick or a backslash either breaks the command or is executed. The only reason for `bash -c` here is the `2>/dev/null`. Separately, the plain (non-`--json`) leg now asserts only `status -eq 1`, which an INCONSISTENT verdict also returns, so despite the comment the usage-error marker is pinned on the `--json` leg alone.
findings.failure_mode: On a host whose `TMPDIR`/`BATS_RUN_TMPDIR` or checkout path contains a shell-significant character the interpolated command fails to parse or runs unintended text, and the test reports a false failure (or, with a crafted path, executes it). The non-JSON leg cannot distinguish a usage error from an INCONSISTENT verdict, so a regression that turned this usage error into a real verdict would pass that leg.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the paths as arguments instead of interpolating: `run bash -c '"$0" --file "$1" --gate review --review-file "$1" --json 2>/dev/null' "$SCRIPT" "$T/r.md"`, or use `run --separate-stderr "$SCRIPT" --file "$T/r.md" --gate review --review-file "$T/r.md" --json` (bats >= 1.5). Optionally assert the usage-error wording on the plain leg's `$output` as well so both paths are pinned by the marker, not the shared exit code.

findings.description: _acl_extended only recognises a POSIX ACL by the presence of the `system.posix_acl_access` xattr. On an NFSv4 mount the Linux client lists `system.nfs4_acl` instead (and never `system.posix_acl_access`), so listxattr succeeds with no POSIX name and the function returns False ("no ACL"). knfsd materialises a named-user write grant as a POSIX ACL on the server, which raises the client-visible S_IWGRP mask bit; the directory then reaches the group-writable branch of _dir_trustworthy, passes the UPG test, and is trusted even though another account has write via the NFSv4 ACL.
findings.failure_mode: A group-writable user-private-group directory on an NFSv4-mounted home (or an NFSv4 TMPDIR) carrying an NFSv4 ACL grant to another user is accepted as an ancestor of the headless CLI's cwd, so that user can plant a CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md on the discovery path. Requires NFSv4 + g+w UPG directory + an explicit ACL grant, so low likelihood.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat `system.nfs4_acl` in the listxattr result as 'no proof' (return True), or refuse the group-writable branch entirely when the filesystem reports any `system.*acl*` name other than a POSIX one. Note the limitation beside the macOS one in the docstring.

findings.description: The new outer `except OSError` turns every OSError that is not FileNotFoundError into `ProviderUnavailableError("... could not prepare its run: ...")`. That label is wrong for exec-time failures that CPython raises with filename=executable: a CLI binary that is present but not executable (PermissionError, EACCES) or an argv that is too long (E2BIG) now reads as a workspace/slot preparation failure. The FileNotFoundError branch already distinguishes a vanished cwd from a missing binary via exc.filename; PermissionError gets no such treatment and never reaches the ConfigError path that carries the `<CLI>_BIN` env hint and install hint.
findings.failure_mode: An operator whose `claude`/`codex` binary lost its execute bit (or whose PATH resolves to a non-executable shim) sees the hop dropped as PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE with 'could not prepare its run: [Errno 13] Permission denied', with no install hint and no pointer to the `*_BIN` override; the companion diagnostic and MODELINV row record a misleading cause. Behaviour is still walkable (an improvement over the previous bare OSError), so this is diagnostic quality only.
findings.suggested_fix: Catch `PermissionError` beside `FileNotFoundError` in the inner try and, when `exc.filename` is not the cwd (reuse cwd_vanished), raise the same ConfigError with the env-name and install hint; alternatively, branch the outer handler on whether `exc.filename` names the executable and word the message 'could not start' for that case.

findings.description: complete() now runs agy in one stable, reused directory (private_workspace("loa-agy-ws")) while passing --dangerously-skip-permissions, and the module docstring states that whether --sandbox blocks writes to that cwd was never probed. The prompt is untrusted review content. If the sandbox permits cwd writes (gemini-cli's sandbox mounts the project dir read-write), a prompt-injected tool call can plant GEMINI.md / .gemini/settings.json in the stable dir, and the next hop starts in that directory. The prior per-hop or caller-cwd layouts did not carry state between hops. The refusal of a stable cwd holding a project file (headless_cli, not in diff) only helps if its list covers agy's own context files, and it then turns one injected write into a permanent refusal of gemini-headless until an operator cleans the directory.
findings.failure_mode: Either persistent cross-hop prompt injection into the Gemini voice (sandbox allows cwd writes and the planted file is not in the refusal list), or a self-inflicted permanent walk of gemini-headless after a single injected write (refusal fires on every later hop with no self-heal).
findings.suggested_fix: At hop start, list the stable dir; if non-empty, log and remove its entries instead of refusing (it is meant to be empty), or recreate it. Add agy's context/config filenames to the refusal list. Make 'sandbox denies writes to cwd' an explicit pass criterion of the T4.1 re-probe before re-enabling agy.

findings.description: sweep_stale_hop_workspaces(base, "loa-grok-ws-") is called inside the staging try whose `except OSError` raises ProviderUnavailableError for this hop. The sweep walks a base shared by every concurrent grok hop (n_slots defaults to 50) and by parallel dissent runs. If two hops sweep the same stale entry and the sweep does not swallow per-entry errors (a stat or rmdir on an entry the other sweeper just removed raises FileNotFoundError, a leftover with a changed mode raises PermissionError), the second hop fails as 'failed to stage isolated workspace' although its own mkdtemp would have succeeded. The sweep's directory scan is also paid on every hop rather than occasionally.
findings.failure_mode: Spurious walkable grok-headless hop failures under concurrent dissents, surfacing as PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE with a misleading 'failed to stage isolated workspace' reason.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the sweep best-effort: catch OSError per entry inside sweep_stale_hop_workspaces and log at debug, and call it outside the try that maps staging errors to a hop failure (or after the hop's own mkdtemp has succeeded). Optionally rate-limit it (e.g., once per process or once per N minutes).

findings.description: Adding cwd=workspace widens the set of OSErrors Popen can raise at spawn: a NotADirectoryError (workspace replaced by a regular file), a PermissionError on chdir, or an ENOENT on a vanished workspace whose filename does not match (cwd_vanished returns False). All but the FileNotFoundError branch fall into the generic `except OSError`, whose message is fixed as 'exec failed (likely ARG_MAX on an oversized prompt)'. That text becomes last_error in the MODELINV row and the dissent envelope's companion diagnostics, so a cwd problem is reported and triaged as an oversized diff.
findings.failure_mode: Misleading operator diagnostics and potential misclassification of the hop's failure in the dissent envelope; the chain still walks, but the recorded reason points at the wrong cause.
findings.suggested_fix: Qualify the message by errno: only E2BIG says ARG_MAX; otherwise report `exec/chdir failed ({errno name}): {exc}` and include exc.filename so a cwd problem is visible.

findings.description: In the cursor adapter the per-hop directory is created by tempfile.mkdtemp and then hold_hop_workspace(workspace) is called, both OUTSIDE the try/finally that owns the rmtree. The codex adapter in the same diff places the hold inside its outer try so its finally always removes the directory. If hold_hop_workspace raises an OSError (os.open or flock failure, e.g. EMFILE under many concurrent hops, or a filesystem that refuses flock on a directory) the freshly created cursor workspace is never removed by this hop.
findings.failure_mode: A hold failure after mkdtemp leaks one 0700 directory under the private base per failed hop. It is only reclaimed by a later cursor hop's sweep once it is a day old, so a burst of hold failures accumulates directories under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or ~/.cache/loa for up to 24 hours. The error itself is still surfaced correctly by the base complete().
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the codex shape: create the workspace and acquire the hold inside the outer try so the finally's shutil.rmtree(workspace, ignore_errors=True) and release_hop_workspace(hold) cover a failing hold. Initialise workspace = None / hold = None before the try and guard the rmtree on workspace is not None.

findings.description: The sandbox warning and the 124 KiB argv refusal are decided from argv alone via _asks_sandbox(command[1:]). The module's own design note states that GEMINI_SANDBOX in the environment outranks --sandbox in gemini-cli. When the operator passes --sandbox in gemini_extra_flags while the ambient environment carries GEMINI_SANDBOX=false or GEMINI_SANDBOX=0 (which _run_subprocess leaves untouched because _asks_sandbox is true), gemini-cli runs with no sandbox and the prompt stays on stdin, yet the hop still logs the exposure warning and refuses any prompt over _SANDBOX_ARGV_CAP.
findings.failure_mode: Under that contradictory but plausible configuration, prompts between 124 KiB and 8 MiB are refused as ProviderUnavailableError before any spawn, dropping the gemini voice from a dissent that gemini-cli would have completed on stdin. The warning also misreports an argv exposure that does not occur.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute the effective sandbox once: treat _asks_sandbox(...) as true only when os.environ.get('GEMINI_SANDBOX', '').strip().lower() is not in ('false', '0') (and optionally when SANDBOX is unset, since gemini-cli never re-sandboxes inside one). Use that single predicate for the warning, the argv cap and the env injection in _run_subprocess so all three agree with what gemini-cli will actually do.

findings.description: The root fixture calls monkeypatch.delenv('XDG_RUNTIME_DIR', raising=False) and the tests then assign os.environ['XDG_RUNTIME_DIR'] = ... directly, relying on the fixture's undo to restore it. pytest's MonkeyPatch.delitem records nothing when the key is absent, so on a host where XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is not set (most CI containers; it IS set on the developer host, which masks this) the direct assignments are never undone and leak into every later test module in the session. The last test in the file leaves XDG_RUNTIME_DIR='run-dir' (a relative path); other orderings leave an absolute path under pytest's basetemp that still exists during the session and would be chosen by private_workspace_base() in unrelated adapter tests.
findings.failure_mode: Order-dependent test pollution: subsequent suites that exercise the real private_workspace_base() (claude, codex, cursor, grok adapter tests) run against a leaked base instead of the host's, which can flip a passing or failing result depending on collection order and whether the host sets XDG_RUNTIME_DIR. Not a production defect, but a flaky-CI source in a suite that pins security behaviour.
findings.suggested_fix: Set the variable through the fixture's monkeypatch everywhere (monkeypatch.setenv('XDG_RUNTIME_DIR', ...) and monkeypatch.setenv('HOME', ...)) instead of assigning os.environ directly, or have the root fixture call monkeypatch.setenv('XDG_RUNTIME_DIR', '') followed by delenv so the key is recorded and restored. Apply the same to the direct HOME assignments for symmetry.

findings.description: The FR-2 entry states the verdict-derive contract as: the trailer is INCONSISTENT when `rejected_summary` is non-empty and "a non-array summary or an unparseable envelope is a violation". The same entry, and the implementation report ("legacy envelopes (no `rejected_summary`, or `null`) pinned as passing"; "a pre-FR-2 envelope ... counts no sidecar rows as old as itself"), say a `null` or absent `rejected_summary` is the legacy pass. `null` is a non-array value, so the published contract sentence contradicts the legacy rule the code implements.
findings.failure_mode: An operator or a downstream check that reads the CHANGELOG as the `verdict-derive.sh` contract expects an envelope with `rejected_summary: null` to fail the trailer check, while the script passes it as a pre-FR-2 envelope. Historical-sprint triage decisions and any tooling built on the stated rule diverge from the code's actual verdict.
findings.suggested_fix: Qualify the sentence: "a present, non-null `rejected_summary` that is not an array, or an unparseable envelope, is a violation; a `null` or absent summary is read as a pre-FR-2 envelope (legacy pass)".

findings.description: The known-failures entry documents a refusal class that did not exist before: `kf-write-lib.sh new` now exits 1 with nothing written for titles that were previously accepted (non-UTF-8, `_emphasis_`, links, HTML tags, character references, backtick runs, padded code spans, a closing `#`, anchor-ambiguous codepoints, and any non-ASCII title when python3 is missing or fails). The entry itself labels this a "Behaviour change" yet is filed under `### Fixed` with no upgrade note, unlike the FR-2 entry directly above it which carries one.
findings.failure_mode: Automation or operators that invoke `kf-write-lib.sh new` with titles in any of the newly refused classes get exit 1 and no ledger entry; a caller that only scans `### Changed` for behaviour changes before upgrading does not learn of the new refusal, and the entry gives no remedy (how to rewrite a refused title, or that python3 is now required for non-ASCII titles).
findings.suggested_fix: Move the behaviour-change sentence under `### Changed` (or add an Upgrade note to the entry) stating that python3 is required for non-ASCII titles and that a refused title must be rewritten in plain text before the entry is written; keep the anchor-slug repair itself under `### Fixed`.

findings.description: The new audit workflow records the verdict with additive labels only: `br label add <task-id> security-approved` or `br label add <task-id> security-blocked`, 'exactly one of' per run. `br label add` never removes the other label, and a sprint task is routinely audited more than once (CHANGES_REQUIRED, then a re-audit that approves — this very sprint has had 38 review rounds). After the second audit the task carries both `security-blocked` and `security-approved`, and the flushed JSONL commits that contradictory state. The reviewing-code copy has the same shape for `review-approved` / `needs-revision` (pre-existing), so any label-driven consumer (ledger, gate, dashboard, `br list --label`) cannot tell the current verdict from the labels.
findings.failure_mode: A task blocked by an earlier audit and approved by a later one (or the reverse) carries both terminal labels; a consumer that checks for `security-blocked` wrongly holds the sprint, one that checks for `security-approved` wrongly passes a task whose latest audit blocked it. The comment line carries the truth but nothing in the workflow says the labels are not authoritative.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the label step idempotent: `br label remove <task-id> security-blocked` before `br label add <task-id> security-approved` (and vice versa), or document that the latest `SECURITY AUDIT:` comment is the source of truth and the labels are advisory. Apply the same to the reviewing-code resource. Keep the added `br label remove` spans inside the skill's `br` allowlist so CMP-188 stays green under `deny_raw_shell`.

findings.description: Flatline's primary (gates prd/sdd/sprint all true) and the Bridgebuilder primary (`@@ -254,7 +261,10 @@`) move to `claude-headless`, and the hunk's own comment states the hop's auth 'follows CLAUDE_HEADLESS_BIN: the claude-bedrock wrapper for Bedrock, else the plain CLI's own login'. Which account pays for every PRD/SDD/sprint Flatline run and every BB sweep is therefore decided by an environment variable at run time, not by the config. The dissent companion in every recent run was pinned to the `claude-bedrock` alias instead, so the two consumers that the comment says share one CLI can in fact run on two different accounts. With `CLAUDE_HEADLESS_BIN` unset (a fresh shell, cron once `scheduling.enabled` flips, a CI runner) Flatline and BB land on the operator's subscription: the plan window of KF-038 and the metering exposure of KF-020.
findings.failure_mode: A Flatline or BB run launched without the wrapper in the environment silently bills the operator's plan and consumes the same window the interactive sessions use; the first symptom is RATE_LIMITED in Flatline Phase 1 followed by the KF-038 breaker cascade into the next dissent, with no config-level indication that the route differed from the intended Bedrock one.
findings.suggested_fix: Pin the route in the config rather than the environment: set `flatline_protocol.models.primary` and the BB primary to the `claude-bedrock` catalog alias the companion already uses (if it passes the BB floor / `isHeadlessModelId` checks), or have the headless adapter fail closed when a Bedrock `compliance_profile` is configured and `CLAUDE_HEADLESS_BIN` does not name the wrapper. At minimum record the resolved binary in the MODELINV row so a plan-billed hop is visible after the fact.

findings.description: The hunk's comment says Flatline 'shares the anthropic headless circuit breaker with the dissent companion: a rate limit on either opens it for both' and treats this as one quota. It is not necessarily one quota: per DISS-002 the Flatline hop may run on the plain CLI (operator plan) while the companion runs via the `claude-bedrock` wrapper (Bedrock, no plan window). The breaker is keyed `anthropic/headless` (`.run/circuit-breaker-anthropic-headless.json`), so a plan-window RATE_LIMITED on Flatline refuses the companion's Bedrock hop that would have succeeded. KF-038's run mode ('wait for the plan window to reset') is then the wrong remedy because the Bedrock route was never limited. This config change is what first puts two auth routes behind one breaker key.
findings.failure_mode: After a Flatline rate limit, the next review's companion is refused as `Circuit open for anthropic/headless` (failure_class model_unavailable), the envelope reads single-voice with `degraded false`, and the operator waits out a plan window that does not gate the companion's actual route. In the unattended harness nothing re-runs the chunk.
findings.suggested_fix: Key the headless breaker by resolved binary or auth route (e.g. `anthropic/headless/<basename of CLAUDE_HEADLESS_BIN>`) or by consumer, as the cycle-end 'per-consumer headless breaker' bead already proposes; until then, state in the KF-038 reading guide that a Bedrock-routed companion refused by the breaker can be re-run at once with `breaker_cli --reset` rather than after the window.

findings.description: `executor_model` and `advisor_model` become the bare alias `fable`, passed verbatim as `claude -p --model fable` by `spiral-harness.sh _invoke_claude`. The comment asserts 'the CLI resolves `fable`' but, unlike the Flatline hunk ('fleet-measured, search 2026-10-01'), cites no measurement. Under the Bedrock route the CLI resolves short aliases through its per-alias default-model env vars, and the comment itself says the harness reaches Bedrock only from a claude-bedrock parent; whether that wrapper maps `fable` to `global.anthropic.claude-fable-5-1` for a child `-p` call is unverified in this diff. The harness is unattended, so an unresolvable alias fails every phase, each retried `max_phase_retries` times.
findings.failure_mode: Every harness phase exits at model resolution (or resolves to a different model than intended), the gate fails after 1 + max_phase_retries attempts, and the only trace is the harness log; the operator reads it as a Bedrock outage rather than a config alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Record one live probe as evidence in the config comment or NOTES: run the harness's exact invocation (`claude -p --model fable` through the claude-bedrock parent) and quote the `model` field the CLI reports. If the alias is not resolved on the Bedrock route, pass the full model id the catalog already carries for `cli_model fable`, or have `_invoke_claude` resolve the alias through the catalog before exec.

findings.description: The new rendered-text guard rejects ordinary underscore emphasis before `gh_anchor` runs, but its regex also matches titles the added tests and comments claim should be accepted, such as `_write_ledger` bounded by spaces.
findings.failure_mode: `op_new` now fails valid titles containing leading/trailing underscores in identifiers. For example `ledger-lib _write_ledger accepts ...` matches `(^|[^[:alnum:]_])_+[^_[:space:]]..._+([^[:alnum:]_]|$)` and exits with the render-diff error, so the new Bats test expecting success will fail and users cannot add such KF entries.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the broad underscore regex with a CommonMark-compatible delimiter check, or explicitly exempt identifier-like underscore pairs that should render literally before treating `_..._` as emphasis.

findings.description: The writer's closing-# check (`cl='(^|[[:space:]])#+[[:space:]]*$'`) runs under LC_ALL=C, so only ASCII space/tab count as whitespace — which is exactly CommonMark's rule for an ATX closing sequence. The lint's equivalent in `rendered_differs` uses Python's Unicode-aware `\s` (`re.search(r"(^|\s)#+\s*$", t)`), which also matches NBSP (U+00A0), U+2000–U+200A, U+3000 etc. A title such as `foo<NBSP>##` or `foo #<NBSP>` is therefore accepted by the writer (correctly — GitHub renders the hashes literally and the raw slug is right) but flagged by `_kf_link_lint`. The other three regex pairs diverge only in the safe direction (the writer is stricter), so this is the single case where the lint is stricter than the writer.
findings.failure_mode: An operator writes an entry whose title holds a Unicode space before a trailing `#`; `kf-write new` succeeds and the Index link is correct on GitHub, but the gating test `every Index link in the shipped ledger names its entry's GitHub heading anchor` goes red on the next CI run, naming a heading that is actually fine.
findings.suggested_fix: In `rendered_differs`, replace `\s` with `[ \t]` in the closing-sequence regex (`(^|[ \t])#+[ \t]*$`) so the lint matches CommonMark and the writer; optionally also pin `[^\s]` → `[^ \t]` in the emphasis `ns` class for symmetry.

findings.description: The non-ASCII path refuses `No` and `Cf` as 'unsettled' but silently drops any code point whose `unicodedata.category` is `Cn` (unassigned in the host Python's Unicode database). The host Python's database lags Unicode (3.12 → 15.0, 3.13 → 15.1, 3.14 → 16.0); a letter assigned in a later version — e.g. a Unicode 16 script character — is `Cn` on an older interpreter and is dropped from the anchor, while GitHub's slugger (newer Unicode) keeps it as a letter. The link lint uses the same host Python so it agrees with the writer, not with GitHub, and the mismatch is invisible to the test suite. This contradicts the function's own rule that a character whose slug the references may disagree on is 'refused, never guessed'.
findings.failure_mode: A title holding a recently assigned letter is written with an anchor missing that character; the Index link resolves to no heading on GitHub, and the ledger lint passes because it shares the stale database.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `"Cn"` to the refusal tuple in `gh_anchor` (`unicodedata.category(c) in ("No", "Cf", "Cn")`) and to `unsettled()` in `_kf_link_lint`, and extend the exit-4 message to name an unassigned character.

findings.description: Sixteen setups (adversarial-review.bats, adversarial-review-e2e.bats, bug-809-status-note.bats, cycle-109-*.bats, cycle-124-dispatch-budgets.bats, cycle-baseline-capture.bats, ledger-isolation-discovery.bats, model-adapter-probe-integration.bats, spiral-harness-adversarial-dissent.bats, wire-schemas-api-safe.bats, input-size-consumers.bats, butterfreezone-gen-sha256-portability.bats, adversarial-review-degraded-on-rejection.bats, adversarial-review-kf-011-debug.bats, adversarial-review-hallucination-filter.bats) export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR" with the comment 'the CLI lock is this test's own, never the per-user one a live dissent holds (run 23)'. The reviewer context for the thirty-eighth run (round 1am, CMP-255) records that the dissent script's locks 'move to a private ~/.cache/loa/headless-locks-<uid>'. If that move made ~/.cache the primary lock base rather than a fallback below $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, every one of these exports is a no-op for lock isolation and the comment is stale: the suites would again resolve the operator's per-user lock directory, which is exactly the queue-behind-a-live-claude.lock failure the run-16/run-23 notes describe (NRM-26). The diff cannot show which reading is right because adversarial-review.sh is not in it.
findings.failure_mode: A suite that reaches a *-headless hop (or whose stubbed hop still takes the per-binary flock) waits up to the lock-wait cap behind a live dissent's claude.lock, or holds that lock and delays the live run; the comment misleads the next reader into assuming isolation that is not there.
findings.suggested_fix: Confirm how adversarial-review.sh resolves the CLI lock directory after CMP-255. If $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is still the first candidate, leave the exports and shorten the comment to cite the resolution order. If ~/.cache/loa/headless-locks-<uid> is now primary, isolate through the script's lock-directory knob (or a per-test HOME) in a shared helper instead of sixteen copies of the export, and have the e3 lint check that knob rather than XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.

findings.description: The e3 lint's patterns have gaps that let the fallback it forbids back in, and one over-match. (1) _e3_xdg_fallback uses 'XDG_RUNTIME_DIR[=][^;]*mktemp': the assign-default form ': "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:=$(mktemp -d)}"' has ':' before '=' and does not match, yet it creates exactly the unswept per-test mktemp directory the lint exists to refuse. (2) _e3_tmpdir_fallback ('[{]BATS_TEST_TMPDIR[:]?[-]') and the case-branch grep ('BATS_TEST_TMPDIR[:]?[-][^}]*mktemp') miss '${BATS_TEST_TMPDIR:=$(mktemp -d)}' for the same reason, and that spelling also satisfies none of _e3_guarded's alternatives, so a suite written that way passes both the guard check and the fallback check while behaving like the old ':-' fallback. (3) '[^;]*' stops only at ';', not at '&&', '||' or '|', so 'export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR" && T="$(mktemp -d)"' is reported as a fallback although the mktemp belongs to another statement, the case the thirty-third-run fix (DISS-C-003) meant to exclude. None of the fixture legs in the test exercise ':=' or an '&&'-joined statement, so the gaps are not pinned.
